sentences.text: Arcticodactylus holds the record for the smallest known pterosaur, with an estimated wingspan of 24 cm.
Its jaws contained eleven or twelve multi-cusped teeth on each side.
Bone proportions indicate the thigh was nearly as long as the upper leg bone, while the upper arm bone was slightly shorter than the thigh.
The shoulder blade was also much longer than the adjacent coracoid bone, measuring 93% of its length.
Analysis of its bone structure suggests the individual was not a newborn but had not yet finished growing.
William Amaral found the fossil site on McKnight Bjerg in eastern Greenland in 1989.
Farish Jenkins and colleagues originally named the species Eudimorphodon cromptonellus in 2001, honoring Professor Alfred Walter Crompton.
Alexander Kellner later established the separate genus Arcticodactylus in 2015.
Researchers proposed that a unique joint in the wing finger represented a transitional form between ancestors with rounded surfaces and later pterosaurs showing a slight depression.
The animal belongs to the class Reptilia and the parent group Pterosauria.
The type species of the genus is Arcticodactylus cromptonellus.
A 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron grouped it within the clade Caviramidae alongside Carniadactylus and Raeticodactylus.
Arcticodactylus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Greenland.
It inhabited the region during the Norian stage, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
It is debated whether Arcticodactylus is closely related to Eudimorphodon, as researchers have noted it lacks key traits like fang-like teeth and striated enamel found in Eudimorphodon.
